content: The circulatory system is an organ system responsible for transporting nutrients, gases, and waste products to and from cells. It also plays a critical role in disease defense, body temperature regulation, and pH stabilization to maintain homeostasis. While it is often viewed as a blood distribution network, it can also be divided into the cardiovascular system, which circulates blood, and the lymphatic system, which circulates lymph. Humans and other vertebrates possess a closed cardiovascular system, meaning blood remains confined within a network of arteries, veins, and capillaries. In contrast, some invertebrates have an open cardiovascular system. Primitive animal phyla lack circulatory systems entirely. The lymphatic system, however, is an open system. The human circulatory system consists of the heart, blood, and blood vessels. It includes two main circuits: the pulmonary circulation, which oxygenates blood in the lungs, and the systemic circulation, which delivers oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. Blood is composed of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Two types of fluids move through the circulatory system: blood and lymph. The cardiovascular system comprises the heart, blood, and blood vessels, while the lymphatic system includes lymph, lymph nodes, and lymph vessels. Together, these systems form the circulatory system. Systemic circulation is the part of the cardiovascular system that carries oxygenated blood from the heart to the body and returns deoxygenated blood back to the heart. Arteries always carry blood away from the heart, while veins return blood to the heart. Typically, arteries carry oxygenated blood, and veins carry deoxygenated blood, except in the pulmonary vessels, where the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs, and the pulmonary vein returns oxygenated blood to the heart. As blood circulates, oxygen and nutrients diffuse from the blood into surrounding cells, while carbon dioxide diffuses into the blood. The release of oxygen from red blood cells is regulated by factors such as increased carbon dioxide levels, higher temperatures, or lower pH, which are characteristic of tissues with high metabolic activity. Pulmonary circulation is the portion of the cardiovascular system that transports deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs and returns oxygenated blood back to the heart. Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium, flows into the right ventricle, and is pumped through the pulmonary arteries to the lungs. Oxygenated blood is then returned to the heart via the pulmonary veins, entering the left atrium and flowing into the left ventricle, from which it is pumped out through the aorta to the rest of the body. The coronary circulation provides blood supply to the heart itself. The heart contains four chambers: the left atrium, left ventricle, right atrium, and right ventricle. These chambers support both systemic and pulmonary circulation. The human cardiovascular system is closed, meaning blood does not leave the network of blood vessels. Oxygen and nutrients diffuse across the vessel walls into interstitial fluid, which delivers them to target cells, while carbon dioxide and waste products move in the opposite direction. The lymphatic system, in contrast, is not closed. In vertebrates, including humans, as well as in annelids (e.g., earthworms) and cephalopods (e.g., squid and octopus), the circulatory system is closed. However, the systems of fish, amphibians, reptiles, and birds exhibit various stages of evolutionary development. Fish have a single circulatory circuit, with blood passing through the gills and body tissues in sequence, supported by a two-chambered heart. Amphibians and most reptiles use a double circulatory system, but their hearts are not always fully divided into two pumps. Amphibians have a three-chambered heart. Birds and mammals have a completely separated four-chambered heart, with independent evolution of this structure in birds and mammals. An open circulatory system, found in animals such as mollusks and arthropods, involves a fluid called hemolymph that bathes organs directly in a cavity called the hemocoel. There is no distinction between blood and interstitial fluid in this system. Hemolymph is composed of water, inorganic salts, and organic compounds such as carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids. Hemocyanin serves as the primary oxygen transporter. Hemocytes, free-floating cells within the hemolymph, play a role in the arthropod immune system. Some animals, such as flatworms, lack a circulatory system. Instead, their branched digestive system facilitates direct diffusion of nutrients to all cells. Their flattened body shape minimizes the distance between cells and the external environment, allowing oxygen to diffuse directly from water into cells and carbon dioxide to diffuse out. This eliminates the need for a transport system. Techniques for measuring circulatory function include electrocardiograms (for cardiac electrophysiology), sphygmomanometers and stethoscopes (for blood pressure), pulse meters (for heart rate and rhythm), and nail bed blanching tests (for perfusion). Vessel cannulation or catheter pressure measurements can assess pulmonary wedge pressure. The history of circulatory system discovery dates back to the 4th century BC, when the valves of the heart were first identified, though their function was not understood. Ancient anatomists believed arteries carried air, as they appeared empty after death. Herophilus distinguished veins from arteries but misunderstood the nature of the pulse. Erasistratus observed that arteries bled when cut during life, hypothesizing the existence of small vessels connecting veins and arteries. Galen, in the 2nd century AD, recognized that blood vessels carried blood and identified venous and arterial blood as having distinct functions. He believed venous blood originated in the liver and arterial blood in the heart, with no return of blood to these organs. In 1242, the Arabian physician Ibn al-Nafis accurately described pulmonary circulation, refuting Galen's idea of invisible pores in the heart's septum. His work was later corroborated by Michael Servetus and Realdo Colombo in the 16th century. William Harvey, in 1628, conducted experiments that led to the discovery of the human circulatory system, publishing a groundbreaking book on the subject. Harvey's work, though initially controversial, eventually gained acceptance. The capillary system connecting arteries and veins was later described by Marcello Malpighi.
